concept.name: Mutual TLS Between Services

relationships.description: Connects Mutual TLS Between Services to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Bidirectional X.509 certificate verification (mTLS) replacing static API keys and IP allowlists with short-lived SPIFFE identities.
concept.purpose: Understand the TLS 1.3 mTLS handshake, automated short-lived certificate rotation, and why SAN-based authorization is mandatory.

spark.summary: Mutual TLS (mTLS) extends standard TLS so both the client and server present and cryptographically verify X.509 certificates during the handshake. In microservice and zero-trust architectures, mTLS replaces fragile static API keys and IP allowlists with automated, short-lived cryptographic workload identities.
spark.keyTakeaway: Standard TLS only authenticates the server; mTLS authenticates both sides, but you still must enforce explicit L7 authorization on the certificate's SAN/SPIFFE URI—signing by a shared CA alone proves membership, not permission.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** In standard TLS, only the server presents a certificate. In **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** (TLS 1.3, RFC 8446), the server sends a `CertificateRequest`, and the client replies with its own `Certificate` and `CertificateVerify` signature.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Bidirectional Certificate Verification + SAN Authorization (Checkout Pod -> Ledger Sidecar -> SPIRE / Mesh CA); Zero-Downtime Intermediate CA Overlap Rotation (TRUST CA1 -> BUNDLE CA1+CA2 -> TRUST CA2).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose between zero-code sidecar automation and direct in-process TLS. Production zero-trust meshes use **SPIRE** (or Istio Citadel/cert-manager) to attest pod identity via the Kubernetes Node API, mint 24-hour X.509 SVIDs in memory (never touching.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore automated TLS rotation, handshake storms, and service mesh architecture.

learningJourney.title: What is Mutual TLS (mTLS)
learningJourney.explanation:
In standard TLS, only the server presents a certificate. In **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** (TLS 1.3, RFC 8446), the server sends a `CertificateRequest`, and the client replies with its own `Certificate` and `CertificateVerify` signature.

In cloud-native meshes, workloads receive automated **short-lived X.509 SVIDs** (1–24 hour TTL) encoding a **SPIFFE URI** (`spiffe://prod.mesh/ns/payments/sa/checkout`) in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN).

sectionDiagram.title: Bidirectional Certificate Verification + SAN Authorization
sectionDiagram.summary: Short 24-hour TTLs rotated in memory eliminate fragile OCSP/CRL revocation checks inside the cluster.

learningJourney.title: Why IP allowlists fail—and the AuthN != AuthZ & CA expiry traps
learningJourney.explanation:
VPC IP allowlists collapse once an attacker compromises one pod and moves laterally, while static API keys leak in logs.

Two production outages dominate mTLS deployments:
- **Missing SAN Authorization (`AuthN != AuthZ`)**: verifying a cert is signed by the corporate CA only proves the caller is in your org—letting a compromised `dev/metrics` pod call the `payments` admin API.
- **Expired Intermediate CA**: leaf certs rotate fine, but an unmonitored intermediate CA expires at 02:00 UTC, taking down 100% of east-west traffic simultaneously.

ideas.title: Enforce Explicit SAN Allowlists
ideas.description: Bind L7 `AuthorizationPolicy` rules to exact `spiffe://` SAN URIs per route.

ideas.title: 2-CA Overlapping Trust Bundles
ideas.description: Alert on CA expiry at 90/30/7 days and rotate intermediate CAs with overlapping trust bundles.

learningJourney.title: Strict mTLS + SAN-Scoped AuthorizationPolicy (Istio)
learningJourney.explanation: Enforce `PeerAuthentication: STRICT` and pair it with an `AuthorizationPolicy` that whitelists exact SPIFFE principals.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: ledger-allow-checkout
  namespace: payments
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: ledger-api } }
  rules:
    - from:
        - source: { principals: ["cluster.local/ns/payments/sa/checkout"] }
      to:
        - operation: { methods: ["POST"], paths: ["/v1/ledger/commit"] }
```

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is verifying that a client's mTLS certificate is signed by your organization's CA NOT sufficient for service-to-service authorization?

options.text: Because TLS 1.3 does not encrypt client certificates
options.feedback: TLS 1.3 encrypts the entire handshake after ServerHello.

options.text: Any compromised pod in the org also has a CA-signed cert; you must inspect the SAN/SPIFFE URI to verify which specific service is calling
options.feedback: Correct: CA validation is Authentication (AuthN); enforcing exact SAN/SPIFFE allowlists per route is Authorization (AuthZ).

options.text: Because short-lived 24-hour certificates skip signature checks
options.feedback: Short-lived certificates undergo full cryptographic verification.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
